1.pericope_label: I declare unto you the gospel which I preached, by which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you

schools.summary: Gill says the apostle here passes to a new subject, the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, which some in this church denied and which he undertakes to prove, establish and defend; and in leading up to it he observes that what he is about to declare is no other than the gospel he had formerly preached to them, which they had received, professed to stand in, and were saved by. The doctrine of the resurrection he calls the Gospel, that being a most important doctrine and a fundamental article of it, and he notes that the resurrection of Christ from the dead made a considerable part in the ministry of the apostles, to the grief of the Sadducees among the Jews, to the scorn of the Gentile philosophers, and to the faith, hope and comfort of Christians. Salvation he takes as inseparably connected with true faith in Christ and with a hearty belief of his rising, which is the earnest and pledge of the rising of the saints. Calvin says the belief of the resurrection among them had been shaken by wicked persons, but leaves it uncertain whether they doubted only the resurrection of the body or the immortality of the soul as well, since some philosophers held souls immortal while the resurrection of the body never entered the mind of any of them, and the Sadducees, with grosser views, thought the soul a breath of wind without substance. He calls the two conditions very cutting, since so sudden a fall proved their knowledge loose and floating.

Henry says it is the apostle's business in this chapter to assert and establish the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, which some of the Corinthians flatly denied. He canvasses how they denied it: whether they turned the doctrine into allegory, as Hymeneus and Philetus did by saying that it was already past, and as several of the ancient heretics did by making it mean no more than a change in the course of life; or whether they rejected it as absurd upon principles of reason and science. His judgment is that they denied it in the proper sense, and that by denying the resurrection of the dead they disowned a future state of recompences. He adds that it does not seem so strange that heathens and infidels should deny this truth, but that Christians, who had their religion by revelation, should deny a truth so plainly discovered is surprising, especially when it is a truth of such importance; and the staggering of their faith made it high time for the apostle to confirm them in it.

Barnes treats the chapter as the third part of the epistle and the most important portion of it, since it contains a connected, laboured and unanswerable argument for the main truth of Christianity and therefore for Christianity itself, and is more interesting to us as mortal beings with an instinctive dread of death than any other part; if the argument is solid then Christianity is true, and it then unfolds the most elevated prospect that can be exhibited to dying yet immortal man. On the clause about being saved he expressly names and rejects the reading of Clarke, Macknight, Whitby and others, that it means only being brought into a salvable state, holding instead that their hopes of eternal life rested on this and that by it they were in fact saved from the condemnation of sin. Robertson notes that the opening verb is used almost as if in reproach, that the gospel is a cognate accusative, and that the relatives run on in asyndeton; both conditional clauses he takes as of the first class, so that the apostle assumes they are holding the word fast while holding the peril over them in their temptation to deny the resurrection. Ellicott sets out the occasion of the chapter, weighs the theory that only a false conception of the resurrection is combated, and decides from the emphatic later statement and the drift of the argument that a flat denial is in view.

Clarke opens with a summary of the whole chapter, the gospel preached, the witnesses of the rising, the apostle's own sight of him and call to the apostleship, the objections answered, the manner in which the great work shall be performed, the astonishing events of the last day, and the use we should make of the doctrine; and he observes that there were false apostles at Corinth who denied the resurrection, in consequence of which three questions are discussed here, whether there be a resurrection of the dead, what will be the nature of the resurrection bodies, and what use is to be made of it all. On the clause about salvation he holds that they are now in a salvable state, saved from their Gentilism and their former sins, and that their future salvation, their being brought finally to glory, will depend on their faithfulness to the grace they have received. Wesley states the same more briefly, that their salvation is begun and will be perfected if they continue in the faith, and that the closing words suppose the alternative that their faith was only a delusion.

Chrysostom explains why the subject comes in at this point and why it is handled with such force. Having finished the discourse of spiritual gifts, the apostle passes to that which is of all most necessary, the subject of the resurrection, for in this too they were greatly unsound. He compares the danger to a fever: as in men's bodies, when it lays actual hold of the solid parts, the nerves and the veins and the primary elements, the mischief becomes incurable unless it receive much attention, so it was likely to happen here, since the mischief was proceeding to the very elements of godliness. Hence the apostle uses great earnestness, for his discourse is henceforth not of morals, not about one man's being a fornicator, another covetous, and another having his head covered, but about the very sum of all good things, the resurrection itself being the point at issue. Because this is all our hope, Chrysostom says, the devil made a vehement stand against this point above others.

Tertullian returns to the resurrection as a subject he has already defended at length. He says that against heretics of all sorts he has given sufficient attention to its defence in another work of his own, but that he will not be wanting in some defence of the doctrine here either, in consideration of such persons as are ignorant of that little treatise. His argument runs to the practice of baptism for the dead, on which he refuses to rest anything: whatever that practice may have been, and whether or not the lustrations of the Romans might be set beside it as prayer for the dead, no one is to suppose that the apostle indicates some new god as the author and advocate of it. His only aim in alluding to it was that he might insist the more firmly on the resurrection of the body, in proportion as they who were vainly baptized for the dead resorted to the practice out of a belief in such a resurrection.

debates: What the Corinthians actually denied: Henry weighs the allegorising of Hymeneus and Philetus against a rejection on principles of reason and decides for a denial in the proper sense, Ellicott reports and rejects the theory that only a refined conception of the resurrection is in view, and Calvin leaves open whether the immortality of the soul was doubted as well as the rising of the body

What being saved by the gospel means here: Clarke takes it of being placed in a salvable state, with final glory depending on faithfulness, Wesley of a salvation begun and to be perfected by continuance, and Barnes expressly names and refuses the first reading, holding that they were in fact saved from the condemnation of sin

How the conditional clauses bear on them: Robertson makes both conditions of the first class, so that the apostle assumes they hold the word fast while holding the peril over them, Ellicott takes the last clause as supposing the impossible case that the whole gospel is false, and Calvin reads both as cutting reproaches of carelessness and fickleness
outliers: Chrysostom compares the spreading error to a fever reaching the solid parts of the body
Barnes says that if the argument of this chapter is solid then Christianity itself is true
Gill notes that the preaching of the resurrection grieved the Sadducees and drew the scorn of the Gentile philosophers
Tertullian refuses to build anything on the practice of baptism for the dead, using it only to press the resurrection of the body

3.pericope_label: Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and was buried, and rose again the third day according to the scriptures

schools.summary: Gill says the phrase means not only first in order but among the chief and principal things, the doctrine of a crucified Christ being what the apostle at first determined only to make known among them, and that he mentions it here in order to lead on to the resurrection, which he then improves in a very strong manner in favour of the rising of the saints. On the burial he collects what the Scriptures had said, that Christ should be in the grave and should make his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death, all of which had their accomplishment through the rich man of Arimathea who begged the body, wrapped it in linen and laid it in his own new tomb; and he adds the type of the prophet three days and three nights in the belly of the fish, according to which our Lord himself foretold it. Since the burial was prophesied of and typified and actually accomplished, it was proper to notice it, both to confirm the certainty of the death and the truth of the rising. Calvin says the apostle confirms what he had stated by explaining that the resurrection was preached by him as a fundamental doctrine of the gospel, laid as a foundation is laid in the erecting of a house, and that he adds to the authority of his preaching by subjoining that he brought forward nothing but what had been enjoined on him by the Lord, delivering it as from hand to hand.

Barnes takes the receiving as a claim to have had these doctrines from the Lord Jesus by inspiration, one instance in which the apostle claims to be under divine guidance, so that they are not to be regarded as his own. On the death for our sins he says the Messiah died as an expiatory offering on their account, that they caused his death and that for them he shed his blood to make expiation, and he calls the passage full proof that Christ did not die merely as a martyr. On the third day he concedes that what the Scriptures foretold was not of necessity the day but the rising itself, and refers to the argument stated in Peter's discourse from the psalm. Ellicott treats the verses as explaining what was meant by the word preached, sets out the historical facts of death, burial and resurrection as the first creed of Christendom, and takes the death as not only because of but in behalf of our sins in order to take them away. He says the burial is emphasised as the proof of the reality of the death, as the entombment of Lazarus shows that he rose from death and not from a trance, and that the reiterated appeal to the Scriptures shows how strongly the apostle dwelt on the unity of the facts with the predictions, the Gospel narratives not yet being in existence. Robertson notes the four items carried by four verbs, cites Stanley and Vincent on whether this is a creed, and insists that the perfect tense of the raising marks its permanence.

Clarke renders the opening as meaning the chief things, or matters of the greatest importance, fundamental truths, and says the doctrine was received by revelations from God himself and not from man. The death of Jesus Christ as a vicarious sacrifice for sin he counts among the things of chief importance and essential to the gospel scheme of salvation. On the third day he meets a difficulty candidly: it is not said anywhere in the Scriptures in express terms that Christ should rise on the third day, but it is fully implied in his types, as in the case of the prophet who came out of the belly of the fish on the third day, and particularly in the case of Isaac, who was a very expressive type, since his being brought to the mount bound and laid on the wood in order to be sacrificed pointed out the death of Christ, and his being brought back pointed out the rising. Wesley says the receiving was from Christ himself and no fiction of the apostle's own, and observes the order of the proof, first from Scripture and then from the testimony of a cloud of witnesses.

Cyril treats the verse as a direction where to look. As the testimonies concerning the Cross were set forth, so now, he says, let us verify the proofs of the Resurrection also, since the Apostle before us affirms that Christ was buried and has been raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. An Apostle having thus sent us back to the testimonies of the Scriptures, it is good that we should get full knowledge of the hope of our salvation. He lists what is to be learned there: first whether the divine Scriptures tell us the season of the Resurrection, whether it comes in summer or in autumn or after winter; then from what kind of place the Saviour has risen, and what has been announced in the admirable Prophets as the name of the place of the Resurrection; and whether the women who sought and found him not afterwards rejoice at finding him. His stated purpose in all this is that when the Gospels are read, the narratives of these holy Scriptures may not be thought fables.

debates: Whether the third day itself was foretold: Clarke concedes it is nowhere said in express terms and rests it on the types of the prophet in the fish and of Isaac, Barnes likewise concedes that what was predicted was the rising rather than its day and appeals to the psalm, while Cyril proposes to search the Scriptures for the very season and place of it

What kind of statement these verses are: Ellicott calls them the first creed of Christendom, Robertson reports Stanley to the same effect but prefers Vincent's judgment that they are a sample of the apostle's early teaching rather than a profession of faith by converts, and Calvin treats them as the foundation laid in the erecting of a house

What the death for our sins secures: Barnes insists the passage proves he did not die merely as a martyr, Clarke calls it a vicarious sacrifice essential to the gospel scheme, Ellicott presses the preposition to mean in behalf of and not merely because of, and Robertson allows that it can carry the sense of instead of
outliers: Robertson observes that the perfect tense of the raising is deliberate: he is still risen
Ellicott compares the entombment of Lazarus, emphasised to show that he rose from death and not from a trance
Gill notes that the burial fulfils the word about a grave with the wicked and with the rich
Cyril's stated aim is that the Gospel narratives should not be thought fables

5.pericope_label: He was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve, then of above five hundred brethren at once, then of James, and last of all of me also

schools.summary: Gill takes Cephas for Simon Peter himself and not, as some had suggested, another of that name among the seventy. He is careful about the order: Peter was not the first person by whom Christ was seen after the resurrection, for he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, but the apostle omits the testimony of the women, and Peter seems to have been the first of the men who saw him risen. The James of the fourth appearance he argues cannot be the son of Zebedee, who had been killed by Herod many years before and so would not be a proper witness to name, but the son of Alphaeus, the brother of our Lord, a man of great fame and credit with the Jews and still living, and therefore a pertinent evidence; the appearance was made to him alone, and though Scripture elsewhere does not mention it there is no room to doubt it, since the apostle here affirms it. Of the apostle's own sight he insists it was corporeal and in heaven rather than on earth, such a one as Stephen had, since otherwise it would have been beside the point to name it among ocular testimonies of the resurrection. Calvin says the apostle brings forward eyewitnesses who saw the accomplishment of what the Scriptures foretold, though not all of them, since the women are unmentioned; he faces the difficulty of the number twelve after the death of Judas and reports an older opinion that the appearance followed the choosing of Matthias, and holds that since the vision granted to the apostle was no deceptive one it was fit to establish belief in the resurrection.

Barnes lays down the principle that the resurrection was a fact to be proved, like all other facts, by competent and credible witnesses, and says the apostle appeals to those who had attested it or yet lived to attest it, showing that it was not possible for so many witnesses to have been deceived; he does not adduce them all, since his purpose was to remind the readers of what they had already heard. He notes that the appearance to the five hundred is omitted by all the evangelists, for reasons unknown, and that the appearance to James is recorded by none of them and survives only in an apocryphal fragment of no authority. Of the last appearance he argues that it proves the apostle saw the same Lord Jesus and the same body the others had seen, since otherwise his assertion would be no proof of the resurrection: it was not fancy, nor imagination, nor even a revelation that Christ had risen, but a real vision of the ascended Redeemer. Ellicott treats the appearances as arranged in chronological order, explains the twelve as a corporate title like the name of a standing council rather than a count of those present, notes that the word for having fallen asleep is the one used of the death of Stephen, and renders the last clause that he appeared last of all as to an untimely born one. Robertson denies that a mere vision is meant, dates the letter not over twenty-five years after the event so that the majority of the five hundred were still living, and gives the literal sense of the last word as a miscarriage.

Clarke reports the textual question at the second appearance, that several manuscripts, the Syriac margin, the Slavonic, Armenian, Vulgate and Italic, and several of the fathers read eleven rather than twelve, a reading supported by one of the Gospels; but he offers the explanation that twelve is used merely to point out the society of the apostles, who though at that time only eleven were still called by their original number, which was afterwards filled up again. Of the five hundred he exclaims at the weight of the testimony, since that many persons saw him at one time and the greater part of them were alive when the apostle wrote, so that he might have been confronted by many had he dared to assert a falsity. He observes further that it seems to have been essential to the character of a primitive apostle that he had seen and conversed with Christ, which the apostle pleaded ever after as proof of his call, and that it does not appear Jesus made any personal discovery of himself to anyone after this. Wesley agrees that the twelve was their standing appellation though the full number was not then present, calls the appearance to the five hundred a glorious and incontestable proof, takes the mention of all the apostles to include the seventy, and says of the closing word that it was impossible to abase himself more, since as an abortion is not worthy the name of a man, so he affirms himself not worthy the name of an apostle.

debates: Whether the twelve is to be read as a number or a title: Clarke records the manuscripts and versions that read eleven and then prefers to take twelve as the name of the society, Wesley calls it their standing appellation, Ellicott makes it a corporate title like that of a standing council, while Calvin faces the arithmetic directly and reports an older solution, that Matthias had already been chosen

Why the women are not among the witnesses: Calvin observes only that the apostle does not adduce them all and makes no mention of the women, while Gill takes the omission as deliberate and infers that Peter was the first of the men, though not the first person, to see the risen Lord

What kind of seeing the apostle's own was: Barnes insists it was a real vision of the ascended Redeemer and not fancy or even a bare revelation that Christ had risen, Gill that it was corporeal and in heaven as Stephen's was, Calvin that it was no deceptive vision, and Clarke that having seen and conversed with Christ was essential to the character of a primitive apostle
outliers: Barnes notes that the appearance to five hundred at once is omitted by every evangelist
Robertson dates the letter within twenty-five years of the event, when most of the five hundred were still alive

Lightfoot traces the word for untimely birth through the Greek version of Job, the Chaldee and the Talmudists, noting that the Greek rendering suggests a birth that went out of the womb while the Hebrew suggests one that never did
Barnes reports that the appearance to James is preserved only in an apocryphal fragment of no authority

9.pericope_label: I am the least of the apostles, because I persecuted the church of God; but by the grace of God I am what I am

schools.summary: Gill says the title refers not to the littleness of the apostle's stature but to the figure just used, and expresses not the opinion of others concerning him but the true and real sense he had of himself, for which he gives the strongest reason that can be given; by apostles he takes him to mean not only the twelve but all other ministers of the Gospel sent forth by Christ. He notes that the same man elsewhere calls himself less than the least of all saints, and yet, when his person and doctrines were traduced by false teachers, defended his standing. On the grace he distinguishes two capacities: privately the apostle was a chosen vessel of salvation, not by works nor on account of faith or any holiness of his, but regenerated, called, sanctified, justified, pardoned and adopted by grace; and as a minister and apostle he was in that high office purely by grace too, not made one by men nor by his education. Calvin doubts whether the confession was drawn out by enemies who made it their aim to detract from his dignity by malicious slander or offered freely, and suspects the former. On the labour he names and refuses the inference that God offers grace while the right use of it remains in man's own power, so that it lies with him to prevent its being ineffectual; the apostle claims nothing here as his own. He notes that the verb for preaching is present, intimating perseverance in teaching the same thing.

Barnes says the self-abasement rests not on any defect in the apostle's commission or any want of qualification to bear witness to what he saw, but on the great crime of his life, the fact that he had been a persecutor, a thing he could never forget, as a man who has been profane and a scoffer can never forget the deep guilt of his former life; the effect is to produce humility and a deep sense of unworthiness ever onward. On the grace he observes that nothing is more common in these writings than a disposition to trace all that he had to the mere mercy and grace of God, and that nothing is a more certain indication of true piety. Of the closing verse he says it is comparatively immaterial by whom the doctrine was established, the great matter being the establishment of the truth. Robertson calls the superlative a true one and not merely intensive, compares the places where the apostle calls himself less than the least of all saints and chief of sinners, and notes that under attack from the Judaizers he still claimed rank equal to any apostle; he takes the relative in the next verse as neuter, meaning what he was rather than who, and says the greater labour is sober fact shown by the Acts and the letters. Ellicott treats the passage as a digression prompted by the memory of the conversion, in which inherent nothingness and greatness by grace are mingled, and says the closing verse recalls the reader to the main argument.

Clarke takes the self-abasement literally, in reference to the apostle's being chosen last and not within the number of the twelve but as an extra apostle, and complains of the pains some men take to make him contradict himself by showing that he was the greatest of the apostles though he calls himself the least; the contradiction is removed by a distinction, since taken as a man and a minister of Christ he was greater than any of the twelve, but taken as an apostle he was less, because not originally in that body, and because none of the twelve had ever persecuted Christ. On the grace he holds that God by his mere grace and good will called him and denominated him an apostle, that he was not unfaithful to the divine call but used the grace given him, and that when his labours, travels and sufferings are considered it is evident he laboured more abundantly than the whole twelve, which was most literally true, though not through his own power or wisdom but through the divine influence that accompanied him. On the last verse he says that all the apostles agree in the same doctrines, that whoever teaches contrary does not preach the true apostolic doctrine, and that the primitive apostles were those who had seen Christ and received their call immediately from himself. Wesley says believers are humbled all their lives even for sins committed before they believed, and traces the greater labour to a deep sense of the peculiar love God had shown him.

Chrysostom reads the three verses as a single manoeuvre and explains its purpose. Having exalted the Apostles and abased himself, and then again having exalted himself above them so that he might make out an equality, since he effected an equality by showing that he had advantages over them as well as they over him, and having thereby proved himself worthy of credit, he does not even so dismiss them, but ranks himself with them again, pointing out their concord in Christ. Yet he does it not so as to seem to have been tacked on to them, but so that he should himself appear in the same rank; for so, Chrysostom says, it was profitable for the Gospel, and the apostle was equally earnest on both sides. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the confession of the persecutor as evidence for the doctrine itself, professing to be filled with wonder at the wise dispensation of the Holy Spirit, who confined the Epistles of the rest to a small number but gave to the former persecutor the privilege of writing fourteen. It was not because Peter or John was less that the gift was restrained; rather, in order that the doctrine might be beyond question, the privilege of writing more was granted to the former enemy, so that all might be made believers, since all were amazed at him and asked whether this was not he who had formerly persecuted.

debates: Whether the apostle's own labour can be credited to him: Clarke says he was not unfaithful to the call but used the grace given, and that his labours prove he wrought more than the whole twelve, Wesley traces the labour to a sense of God's peculiar love while ascribing the power to grace, and Calvin expressly names and rejects the inference that God offers grace while its right use remains in man's own power

Why the self-abasement is made at all: Calvin suspects it was drawn out to answer slanderers, Barnes lays it wholly to the memory of the persecution, Clarke takes it as literally true of one chosen last and outside the twelve, and Ellicott treats it as an outburst of personal feeling in a digression

How the least of the apostles can also claim to have laboured most: Clarke distinguishes the man and minister from the apostle, Robertson notes that the same writer defended his rank as equal to any apostle when the Judaizers attacked, and Chrysostom explains the whole as a deliberate movement from abasement to equality and then to concord
outliers: Cyril of Jerusalem finds it a work of the Spirit's wisdom that the former persecutor was given fourteen epistles to write while the rest wrote few
Barnes says the trait of tracing everything to God's mercy is itself a certain indication of true piety
Robertson observes that the relative is neuter, naming what the apostle was rather than who he was
Clarke defines the primitive apostles as those who had seen Christ and received their call immediately from him

12.pericope_label: How say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there be no resurrection, then is Christ not risen; and if Christ be not risen, our preaching is vain

schools.summary: Gill takes the denial at its widest, that there is no such thing as a resurrection of any, that the thing is not possible, and that it never has been, is, or will be true in fact; on that supposition, he says, it must be granted that Christ is not risen either. Calvin explains the logic of the whole passage: a mutual and reciprocal inference holds good on the one side and on the other, both affirmatively and negatively, arguing from Christ to us and from us to Christ. The ground of the argument from Christ to us is that he did not die or rise again for himself but for us, so that his resurrection is the foundation and substance of ours, and what was accomplished in him must be fulfilled in us also. On the consequence he presses the word for vain as far as it will go: the preaching would be empty not simply as having some mixture of falsehood but as being altogether an empty fallacy, for what remains if Christ has been swallowed up by death, if he has become extinct, if he has been overwhelmed by the curse of sin, if he has been overcome by Satan? If that fundamental article is subverted, all that remains will be of no moment; and there can be no solidity of faith where no hope of life is to be seen, since in the death of Christ considered by itself, apart from the rising, nothing is seen but ground of despair.

Henry says that having confirmed the truth of our Saviour's resurrection the apostle goes on to refute those among the Corinthians who said there would be none. From this passage and the course of the argument it seems there were some among them who thought the resurrection an impossibility, which was a common sentiment among the heathens; and against this the apostle produces an incontestable fact, namely the resurrection of Christ, and then goes on to argue against them from the absurdities that must follow from their own principle. The method is what Henry chiefly notices: the fact is set down first and the consequences of denying it are drawn out afterwards, one absurdity after another, so that the denial is refuted not by assertion but by what it destroys.

Barnes says the apostle, having stated the direct evidence for the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, now demonstrates that the dead will rise by showing how this follows from that fact and what consequences would attend denying it, the whole argument being based on the one event; if that is admitted, it follows that his people will rise too. On the reversed inference he presses the physical difficulty: the same obstacles stood in the way of raising him as in any other case, since he was dead and buried, had lain in the grave three days, the human soul had left the body, the frame had become cold and stiff, the blood had ceased to circulate and the lungs to heave, so that if raising the dead is held impossible and absurd, he has not been raised. On the word vain he includes the ideas of useless, idle and false, since it would be false to affirm that the system was from heaven and useless to proclaim one that could save no one. Ellicott states the matter as logic, that a man has been proved by historical evidence to have risen and it is therefore illogical to deny that the dead rise, and traces the chain from preaching to faith to delusion. Robertson notes the personal use of the verb, identifies the objectors as sceptics who deny the resurrection as others deny miracles, and says the argument is turned round with tremendous force, adding that it is fair.

Clarke reasons from what they had already accepted: seeing that Christ was so preached and the preaching credited, how do some among them, who professed to receive the doctrine from the apostles, say that there is no resurrection of the dead, when his resurrection has been shown to be the proof and pledge of ours? He suspects a particular source for the error, that there was some false teacher among them endeavouring to incorporate Mosaic rites and ceremonies with Christian doctrine and even to blend the tenets of the Sadducees with the whole, and says the chapter was written to confute this mongrel Christian and overturn his bad doctrine. He observes further that there seem to have been some at Corinth who denied the resurrection of the dead while admitting that Christ had risen, and meets them by pointing out that Christ was partaker of the same flesh and blood with us: if he was raised, mankind may be raised, and if mankind cannot be raised, then his body never was. The consequence he states flatly, that the whole doctrine would be useless, nugatory and false, and the belief of a false doctrine necessarily unprofitable. Wesley supposes the objectors had probably been heathen philosophers, calls their view a flat impossibility, and observes that the preaching rests on a commission given after the resurrection.

debates: Who denied the resurrection at Corinth: Henry and Wesley take them for men carrying over the common sentiment of the heathen, Wesley guessing they had been philosophers, Clarke suspects a single false teacher blending Mosaic rites and Sadducean opinions into Christian doctrine, and Robertson simply calls them sceptics of the kind who now deny that miracles happen

Whether some admitted Christ's rising while denying ours: Clarke says there seem to have been such at Corinth and answers them from the shared flesh and blood, while Barnes argues that the physical difficulty is identical in both cases, so that denying one denies the other

How far the word vain reaches: Barnes takes it to include useless, idle and false, Robertson glosses it as empty, Clarke calls the doctrine nugatory, and Calvin presses it hardest, making the preaching not a mixture of falsehood but an entire fallacy and the faith without solidity where no hope of life appears
outliers: Robertson calls the reversal of the argument tremendous in force and adds that it is fair
Barnes lists the physical marks of death in the case of Christ to show the difficulty was the same as in any other
Calvin observes that the inference runs both ways, from Christ to us and from us to Christ, affirmatively and negatively
Henry notes that the refutation proceeds by drawing absurdities out of the objectors' own principle

15.pericope_label: We are found false witnesses of God; if Christ be not raised, ye are yet in your sins, and they which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished

schools.summary: Gill says the apostles were chosen to be witnesses of the resurrection, that Christ appeared to them for this very purpose, and that they were sent into all the world to bear their testimony to it; so that if Christ is not risen they have borne a false testimony, and no more odious character can be fixed upon a man than that of a false witness. He observes that the repetition of the argument is made partly to show its importance and partly to bring out further absurdities that follow from it, and that the faith called vain is not only the doctrine of faith but the grace of faith, the faith of God's elect, the pure gift of his grace and the operation of his power, which Christ is the author and finisher of, so that to call it vain is the height of absurdity. Of those fallen asleep he reports that some understand only such as died martyrs for Christ and his Gospel, but holds that all believers are designed. Calvin allows that the consequences named earlier were more serious as regards us, but counts it no trivial absurdity that the Apostles, ordained by God to be heralds of his eternal truth, should be detected as men who had deceived the world with falsehoods, since this tends to God's highest dishonour. He grants all that the death accomplished and then withdraws it, since none of it would have stood had Christ not by rising come off victorious; if the resurrection is overthrown, the dominion of sin returns.

Barnes says the apostles would be proved to have affirmed of God what is not true, and that nothing could be regarded as a greater crime, whatever the immediate subject. He treats the repeated verse as repeated for its importance, explains that the faith would be vain because those holding it would still be unpardoned sinners, since the pardon of sin is bound up with belief in the rising, and states the further consequence that all Christians who had died would have failed of salvation, having fixed all their hopes on a risen Saviour. On the last verse he reports that Doddridge, Macknight, Grotius and others refer the pity to the apostles only, as men who had exposed themselves to a peculiar variety of dangers and trials. Ellicott insists that the apostles would be not mistaken but lying witnesses, not deceived but deceivers, and points out the suppressed premise, that there was no motive for them to speak untruth; he also marks the change of method at the repeated verse, where the historical argument being complete the apostle turns to a reduction to absurdity. Robertson weighs the genitive as either subjective or objective and prefers to take the following preposition as against God, notes that the second word for vain is stronger than the first, meaning devoid of truth, and observes that if hope is limited to this life we have denied ourselves what people call pleasures and have nothing beyond, so that the Epicureans have the argument on us.

Clarke turns the charge of false witness into a practical test: the apostles testified the fact as a matter they had themselves witnessed, and if that were false, could five hundred persons agree in the imposition, and if they did, is it possible that no one would discover the cheat, when he could have no interest in keeping the secret and might greatly promote his secular interest by making the discovery? Such a case, he says, never occurred and never can occur. On the remaining in sin he argues backwards: if Christ has not risen there is no proof that he was not justly put to death, since God would not work a miracle to raise a malefactor, and if he was justly put to death he has made no atonement, so that his readers are still under the power, guilt and condemnation of their sins. Of the dead he says that all who by martyrdom or natural death departed in the faith are perished, their bodies dissolved in the earth notwithstanding the promise to raise them at the last day. The last verse he would repunctuate and render, that if in this life we have hoped in Christ only we are more to be pitied than all men, since we have denied ourselves and been denied by others. Wesley holds that more than the reformation plainly wrought in them was needed, even the atonement whose sufficiency God attested by raising our great Surety from the grave, and answers the last verse by pointing to a hope full of immortality, which makes believers happier than all men in spite of present trials.

debates: What the false witness would amount to: Ellicott insists it would be deliberate lying rather than honest error and rests on the absence of any motive, Clarke tests it by asking whether five hundred could keep such a secret against their own interest, Robertson weighs whether the testimony would be in God's service or against him, and Calvin measures the absurdity by the dishonour it brings on God

Why the readers would still be in their sins: Barnes ties pardon to belief in the rising, Robertson denies the death any atoning value apart from it, Clarke argues that an unrisen Christ would be presumed justly executed and so no atonement at all, and Calvin grants everything the death accomplished only to withdraw it for want of the victory

Whom the pity of the last verse falls on: Barnes reports the view of Doddridge, Macknight and Grotius that only the apostles are meant, while Clarke and Robertson take the clause generally and make the word only govern the whole, and Wesley reverses it by appealing to a hope full of immortality
outliers: Clarke argues that no conspiracy of five hundred could have held, since any one of them could have profited by exposing it
Robertson concedes that on the sceptics' premise the Epicureans have the argument on us
Gill reports that some limited those fallen asleep to the martyrs, naming Stephen and James
Calvin says it were better not to believe at all, the condition of unbelievers being preferable, if hope ends at death

20.pericope_label: But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept: for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive

schools.summary: Gill says the fact was proved before by ocular testimonies and preached and asserted, and is now reassumed and concluded from the glaring contradictions and dreadful absurdities that follow its denial. On the first man he explains that sin was the cause of death, of its coming into the world and upon all men, and that since the apostle is treating of the resurrection of the body a bodily death seems chiefly intended, though the first man also brought a moral death and a liability to eternal death. He explains the two representative relations: all men were in Adam seminally, as the common parent of human nature, in the way that Levi was in the loins of Abraham when Melchizedek met him, and representatively, Adam being the federal head of all his posterity and so a type and figure of Christ that was to come, so that being in him they all sinned in him and died in him. Calvin states the point to be proved, that Christ is the firstfruits and was not raised merely as an individual, and proves it from contraries, since death is not from nature but from man's sin: as Adam did not die for himself alone but for us all, so Christ, the antitype and first pattern of the resurrection set against the death of Adam, did not rise for himself alone, but came to restore everything that had been ruined. He notes the force of the argument, which proceeds not by similitude or example but by something stronger.

Henry says the apostle here establishes the truth of the resurrection of the dead, the holy dead, the dead in Christ, upon the resurrection of Christ himself, and first because he is indeed the firstfruits of those that slept. He has truly risen himself, and he has risen in this very quality and character, as the firstfruits of those who sleep in him. Henry draws the force of the figure from the law of the offering: as the whole lump was made holy by the consecration of the firstfruits, so in the resurrection of Christ there is as much an earnest given that the dead in him shall rise as there was that the Jewish harvest in general should be accepted and blessed by the offering and acceptance of the firstfruits. What is proved thereby is not a bare possibility but a pledge, and it belongs to the whole body of Christ, all that are his.

Barnes hears in the verse the bursting forth of a full heart and of overpowering conviction, as though the apostle were impatient of the slow process of argument, weary of meeting objections and stating consequences, and longing to utter what he knew, since he had seen the risen Lord and could no more doubt this than any other fact he had witnessed with his own eyes. On the first man he holds that death would not have entered the world had it not been for transgression, so that man would have remained immortal on the earth or been translated to heaven as Enoch and Elijah were, without seeing death; and he guards the clause about dying in Adam, since men did not become actually dead when Adam sinned, having then no existence, but the death of all is traced to him as the procuring cause. Ellicott sets the turn of thought, that from the ghastly conclusion of the hypothesis the apostle turns to hopeful faith; he explains that the firstfruit must be a sample of the same kind as what it represents, that Christ rose to the inclusion and not the exclusion of humanity, and that his federal relation to mankind is not dated from the incarnation. Robertson calls the verse the logical triumph after the reduction to absurdity, notes that others raised from the dead died again while Jesus did not, derives our word for a cemetery from the verb for sleeping, and admits the difficulty of fixing how far the second all extends.

Clarke says the resurrection of Christ has been demonstrated and ours necessarily follows, since as surely as the firstfruits are proof that there is a harvest, so surely is his rising a proof of ours. He quotes Lightfoot at length on the offering of the sheaf and remarks that the Judaizing teacher at Corinth would feel the force of the observation much sooner than we can, who are not much acquainted with Jewish customs. Of the two men he says in a line that mortality came by Adam and immortality by Christ, so that as surely as all have been subjected to natural death by the one, so surely shall all be raised again by the other, mortality and immortality on a general ground being the subject of the reasoning here. Wesley says the apostle now declares that Christians have hope and not in this life only, and observes that the proof of the resurrection lies in a narrow compass while almost all the rest of the chapter is taken up in illustrating, vindicating and applying it. He calls the firstfruits the earnest, pledge and insurance of the resurrection of those who slept in him, even of all the righteous, and holds that it is of the resurrection of these only that the apostle speaks; the second clause he reads carefully, since it does not say they shall revive, as naturally as they die, but that they shall be made alive by a power not their own.

debates: How far the second all reaches: Wesley limits the being made alive expressly to the righteous and stresses that they do not revive of themselves but are made alive by a power not their own, Robertson allows that the two companies may not coincide and that the verb means restoration to life rather than salvation, while Ellicott divides the inheritance itself, the fleshly from the one and the spiritual from the other

What the figure of the firstfruits proves: Henry takes it from the consecration of the lump as an earnest that the dead in Christ shall rise, Clarke as proof that there is a harvest, Ellicott as requiring that the sample be of the same kind as what it represents, and Wesley as the pledge and insurance of the rising of the righteous

Why the death of one man reaches all: Gill grounds it on the seminal and federal presence of all men in Adam, Calvin on the fact that death is not from nature but from sin, so that the antitype answers the type, and Barnes on Adam's act as the procuring cause, denying that men died actually when they did not yet exist
outliers: Lightfoot dates the rising by the calendar of the sheaf offering: Passover, then the sabbath, then the firstfruits
Ellicott suggests the letter may have been written near Passover, which would explain the choice of the image
Robertson notes that others raised from the dead died again, but not Jesus, and derives our word cemetery from the verb for sleeping
Barnes holds that but for transgression man would have remained immortal on earth or been translated as Enoch and Elijah were

23.pericope_label: Every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming; then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom

schools.summary: Gill rules out the wrong senses of order: not order of time, as if the saints of the first age should rise first and then those of the next; nor of dignity, as martyrs in the rank of martyrs and preachers in the rank of preachers; nor of age, the elder before the younger; nor of state and condition, married persons and virgins each in their own rank. Of the end he says it is the end of all things, the end of the righteous being peace and everlasting joy and uninterrupted communion with Christ, and the end of the wicked destruction and everlasting punishment. Of the reign he says Christ must reign because it is the unalterable will and unchangeable decree of God that he should, because he has promised it and prophesied of it. The last enemy he takes to be not eternal death, since the wicked will always be subject to that, but a corporeal death, which is an enemy as the fruit, effect and wages of sin, the penalty and curse of the law, contrary to human nature and destructive of the work of God's hands. Calvin reads the passage as anticipating an objection, that if the life of Christ draws ours along with it, why does this not appear, since he has risen while we lie rotting; the answer is that God has appointed another order, and it is enough that we now have the firstfruits in Christ. He adds that the Father placed him at his right hand with the understanding that he should not resign the authority received until his enemies were subdued, and that this is said for the consolation of the pious against impatience at the long delay.

Barnes explains the word for order from military usage, the arrangement of a cohort properly marshalled with the officers at the head and every man in his proper place in the ranks, and thinks the design is partly to counteract the notion that the resurrection was already past. He takes the end as the completion of the work of redemption, the winding up of the affairs conducted under the mediatorial reign rather than something following it, and the necessity of the reign as one of propriety and of what had been contemplated and predicted. On the last enemy he holds that the other foes are subdued earlier, the enmity of the human heart by the triumphs of the gospel, the sceptre of Satan wrested from him, the false systems of religion destroyed, so that nothing remains but death, which the resurrection overcomes. Ellicott sets out the three groups and observes that the interval between the second and third, its length and how it is spent, is not spoken of here, the only point being the order; he extends the rule to be abolished beyond hostile power to all intermediate rule of any sort, good and bad, and argues that the reign was prophesied because it is morally necessary rather than being necessary because prophesied. Robertson gives the military sense of the word for order, notes that the word for the coming was the technical term for a royal or imperial visit, with advent-coins struck afterwards, observes that the construction is indefinite as to time, and gives the literal order of the last clause.

Clarke numbers three orders, Christ who rose by his own power, then those who are his, all his apostles, martyrs, confessors and faithful followers, and then the end when the whole mass shall be raised; but he adds candidly that he will not assert this to be exactly what the apostle intends, though of the first there can be no question. The kingdom delivered up he defines as the mediatorial kingdom, which comprehends all the displays of grace in saving sinners and all spiritual influence in governing the Church, and he takes the rule and authority and power to refer to earthly governments as well as to spiritual wickedness. On the reign he rests everything on the promise, holding that the kingdom cannot be given up till all rule and government are cast down, so that while the world lasts all human beings are properly his subjects and accountable to him. Of the last enemy he says the verb means to be counter-worked, subverted and finally overturned, and reasons that death cannot be destroyed by there simply being no further death, but only by a general resurrection, so that the promised destruction both assures that resurrection and proves that after it there shall be no more death. Wesley notes that the wicked rise at the same time though not here taken into the account, guards the surrender of the kingdom by observing that the Father does not then begin to reign without the Son nor the Son cease to reign, and orders the three enemies historically, since Satan brought in sin and sin brought forth death.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse against a particular error and names its source. He asks how those who teach the contrary ran into such madness, and answers that they read wrongly that good word of the Apostle, that he must reign till he has put all enemies under his feet; from this they say that when his enemies have been put under his feet he shall cease to reign, alleging it wrongly and foolishly. Cyril's reply is a single argument from the greater to the less: he who is king before he has subdued his enemies, how shall he not the rather be king after he has gotten the mastery over them? The word till, on his reading, marks the completion of the subjection and not a term set to the kingdom, so that the very clause the objectors seize upon tells against them.

debates: Why Christ must reign until the subjection is complete: Wesley and Clarke rest it on the written promise, Ellicott expressly reverses the order and says it was prophesied because it is morally necessary rather than necessary because prophesied, Barnes takes the word of propriety, and Calvin makes it the terms on which the Father seated him at his right hand

What rule is abolished at the end: Clarke takes it of earthly governments and spiritual wickedness alike, Ellicott extends it to all intermediate rule of any sort, good as well as bad, since God is at last to govern his creatures directly, and Wesley limits the surrender to the mediatorial kingdom, denying that the Son then ceases to reign

What kind of death is the last enemy: Gill excludes eternal death, since the wicked remain under it, and takes the corporeal death alone, while Clarke argues that death cannot be abolished by mere cessation but only by a general resurrection, and Wesley sets it third after Satan and sin in the order both of conquest and of invasion
outliers: Robertson notes that the word for the coming was the technical term for a royal visit, after which advent-coins were struck
Clarke declines to insist that his own threefold order is exactly the apostle's
Ellicott says humanity, having shared the condition of fallen Adam, will be restored to the state of unfallen Adam and ruled by God face to face
Cyril of Jerusalem answers those who inferred from the word till that the reign of Christ will one day end

27.pericope_label: He hath put all things under his feet; and when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject, that God may be all in all

schools.summary: Gill takes the quoted words as proof that all enemies and death itself shall be put under the feet of Christ, and denies that they can be understood of Adam in a state of innocence, since the word used there signifies a frail mortal man, which he then was not, nor could he be called the son of man; and though the earth was subdued to him and he had dominion over the fish and the fowls and every living thing, the creatures were not subject to him in the large sense in which the apostle explains the words. On the subjection he observes that all things are not as yet put under Christ in fact, though in right God the Father has given him an authoritative power over all things and a right to dispose of them at his pleasure, and that the full subjection waits until the last enemy is destroyed. Calvin allows that the quotation is probably from the psalm and faces the two difficulties in applying it: that the prophet speaks there not of Christ alone but of the whole human race, and that by all things he means only such things as serve the convenience of the life of the body. On the last clause he asks whether God will be all in all in the Devil and wicked men also, and answers that he will not in the ordinary sense; at present, while the Devil resists God and wicked men confound the order he has established, it does not distinctly appear, but when Christ has executed the judgment committed to him and cast down Satan and all the wicked, the glory of God will be conspicuous even in their destruction.

Barnes says the apostle refers to some promise or prediction concerning the Messiah without expressly quoting one or making it certain what he has in view, and notes that the words occur in a psalm as applicable to man and designed to show the dignity and dominion of man, so that whether that psalm has any reference to the Messiah has been made a question. On the subjection of all things he reads the future tense as implying that the time has not yet arrived, the dominion being now exercised while the plans move forward toward the subjugation of all things to God. Ellicott makes the verse about death a parenthesis, so that the connecting word goes back to the reign, and treats the psalm as an Old Testament statement about man applied to Christ as the Son of Man, comparing similar applications elsewhere; of the closing phrase he says it expresses the complete redemption both of the race and of the individual and is the sublime conclusion to which the moral enthusiasm and earnest logic of the argument has necessarily brought us. Robertson supplies God as the subject of the first verb, allows either God or Christ as the subject of the second, notes that the perfect passive marks a state of completion and final triumph, complains that the aorist subjunctive has given translators a deal of needless trouble, and calls the last clause the final goal of all God's redemptive plans.

Clarke says the Father has put all things under the feet of Christ according to the prophecy, and that the exception of the Father is introduced to show that the apostle does not mean the divine nature to be subjected to the human: Christ, as Messiah and Mediator between God and man, must ever be considered inferior to the Father, and his human nature, however dignified by its union with the divine, must ever be inferior to God; the whole verse he would read in a parenthesis. On the subjection of the Son he fixes the moment precisely, that when the administration of the kingdom of grace is finally closed, when there shall be no longer any state of probation and consequently no longer need of a distinction between the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of glory, then the Son, as being man and Messiah, shall cease to exercise any distinct dominion, and the one infinite essence shall appear undivided and eternal. Wesley states the surrender in a phrase, that the Son delivers up the mediatorial kingdom, and expands the closing words to mean that all things, and consequently all persons, without any interruption, without the intervention of any creature and without the opposition of any enemy, shall be subordinate to God, all saying, my God and my all; this is the end, and even an inspired apostle can see nothing beyond this.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses both verses against those who drew wrong conclusions from them. On the first he insists that the Lord says this to the Lord, not to a servant but to the Lord of all and his own Son, to whom he put all things in subjection; the Only-begotten Son is Lord of all and yet the obedient Son of the Father, for he did not grasp the Lordship but received it by nature of the Father's own will, neither did the Son grasp it nor the Father grudge to impart it. On the second he reports that some have dared to say that the words show the Son shall be absorbed into the Father, and calls the saying blasphemous. His answer is a pair of questions. Shall the creatures of Christ continue, and shall Christ perish, by whom both they and all things were made? And how shall all things be made subject to him, by perishing or by abiding? If the other things abide when subject to the Son, it cannot be that the Son fails to abide when subject to the Father; the subjection therefore marks not a ceasing to be but an order within what continues.

debates: Whom the quoted psalm speaks of: Barnes reports that whether it refers to the Messiah has been made a question and that the apostle names no passage, Calvin states the difficulty that the prophet speaks of the whole human race and of bodily conveniences only, Gill argues from the very words that Adam in innocence cannot be meant, and Ellicott takes it as a statement about man applied in a higher sense to the Son of Man

What the subjection of the Son amounts to: Clarke dates it from the closing of the kingdom of grace and confines it to the Son as man and Messiah, Wesley calls it the delivering up of the mediatorial kingdom, and Cyril of Jerusalem answers those who inferred from it that the Son will be absorbed into the Father, arguing that things subjected abide rather than perish

How far God is all in all: Ellicott and Wesley take the phrase for the complete and unhindered subordination of all persons and things, Robertson calls it the final goal of the redemptive plans, while Calvin denies that it holds of the Devil and the wicked in the same sense and locates the glory of God in their destruction
outliers: Clarke would read the whole verse about the exception in a parenthesis, and Ellicott the verse before it
Robertson says the aorist subjunctive here has given translators a deal of needless trouble
Cyril of Jerusalem argues that the Son neither grasped the Lordship nor did the Father grudge to impart it
Wesley says that even an inspired apostle can see nothing beyond this end

29.pericope_label: What shall they do which are baptized for the dead? Why stand we in jeopardy every hour? I die daily. If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus

schools.summary: Gill says the apostle returns here to his subject and uses new arguments, but confesses that his sense is not easy to understand, nor what rite or custom or action he refers to, which must be either one of the divers Jewish washings, or Christian baptism literally taken, or baptism in a figurative and metaphorical sense. On the danger he extends the reproach beyond those who suffered martyrdom to ministers and private Christians on the spot, who continually expose themselves and are every moment liable to injuries, tortures and death, asking who in his senses would act such a part if there is no resurrection of the dead. On the beasts at Ephesus he reports the figurative readings, that by beasts are meant Satan, the roaring lion, and his principalities and powers, or men of savage disposition and persecuting principles, one ruler having been called a fox and another a lion, so that the fighting would be the apostle's disputes with hardened and unbelieving Jews. Calvin says the apostle resumes his enumeration of the absurdities, having interrupted the thread with instruction and consolation, and that he first objects that the baptism of those already reckoned as dead is of no avail without a resurrection; he sets aside the common exposition before giving his own. On the danger he speaks of voluntary perils, into which believers throw their lives for the confession of Christ, and says that such magnanimity in despising death would be ascribed to rashness rather than firmness if the saints perished at death.

Barnes says the argument interrupted earlier is here resumed, and admits that there is perhaps no passage in the New Testament over which there has been a greater variety of interpretation, the views of expositors by no means harmonizing even now. On the daily peril he says the apostles constantly risked their lives by land and sea in the arduous work of making the gospel known, and that such efforts would be vain, useless and foolish unless a glorious resurrection awaited; the oath he calls a particle of swearing denoting a strong asseveration, and he reports that many manuscripts read our rejoicing though the received reading is your. Ellicott imagines the apostle pausing for breath after the outburst of mingled rhetoric and logic, or postponing the dictation, so that the abruptness is less startling; he marks the strong contrast between them in one verse and we in the next, takes the converts themselves as the boast sworn by, and calls such a life a daily dying. Robertson reports that Stanley lists thirteen interpretations of the baptism and that over thirty have been proposed, gives the reading of the Greek expositors, notes that there is no word for protest and that the oath is carried by a particle, observes that the apostle was never out of danger from Damascus to Rome, and objects to the literal fighting with beasts that a Roman citizen could not lawfully be so treated.

Clarke calls this certainly the most difficult verse in the New Testament, since notwithstanding the labours of the greatest and wisest men there are nearly as many different interpretations of it as there are interpreters, and declines to rehearse the discordant opinions. On the daily danger he asks whether there is any reason to submit voluntarily to so many sufferings if the dead rise not, and answers that they had counted the cost, despised sufferings and exulted at the prospect of death because they knew they should have a resurrection unto eternal life. On the oath he follows Lightfoot, understanding the boasting of the Corinthians' boasting against the apostle, so that he considered himself continually trampled on, rejected and exposed to infamy and contempt, but took this as part of the reproach of Christ. On the beasts he argues that the fight was not literal, both from the apostle's own silence when enumerating his sufferings elsewhere and from the silence of his historian. Wesley offers two senses of the disputed baptism, either in hope of blessings to be received after being numbered with the dead, or in the room of the dead, of those just fallen in the cause of Christ, like soldiers who advance into the place of companions that fell before their face; the beasts he takes for a proverbial phrase expressing the most imminent danger, namely the savage fury of a lawless multitude.

Chrysostom explains the method before touching the sense. The apostle takes in hand another topic, establishing what he says at one time from what God does and at another from the very things which his hearers themselves practise; and this, he observes, is no small plea in the defence of any cause, when a man brings forward the gainsayers themselves as witnessing by their own actions to what he affirms. Before giving his own account of the disputed words, Chrysostom proposes to mention first how those infected with the Marcionite heresy pervert the expression, and says frankly that he knows he will excite much laughter by rehearsing it, but that even on this account it should be told. The point of the argument, as he takes it, is that the practice of the objectors bears witness against their own doctrine.

debates: What the baptism for the dead means: Lightfoot takes baptism for martyrdom, Wesley offers either a baptism in hope of blessings after death or one in the room of the fallen, Gill leaves the choice open among Jewish washings, literal baptism and a figure, Calvin refers it to those already reckoned as dead, while Robertson reports over thirty proposals and the Greek expositors' reading that it means about the dead

Whether the fighting with beasts was literal: Lightfoot holds that the apostle was really cast to wild beasts in the theatre and answers the silence of the historian by his many other omissions, Clarke argues from that same silence and the apostle's own that it was figurative, Robertson objects that a Roman citizen could not lawfully be so treated, Wesley takes it for a proverb of imminent danger, and Gill for savage men

Whose boasting is sworn by: Barnes notes the manuscripts divided between your and our and keeps your, Ellicott takes the converts themselves as the boast, while Lightfoot and Clarke understand instead the Corinthians' boasting against the apostle, which he bore as part of the reproach of Christ
outliers: Chrysostom observes that it is no small plea to bring forward the gainsayers themselves as witnesses by their own practice
Ellicott imagines the apostle pausing for breath, or postponing his dictation to another day, before this abrupt new argument
Robertson mentions that a place in the ruins of Ephesus is still called the prison of Paul
Calvin corrects Erasmus, that those meant are not men thrown to the beasts but men condemned to fight them

33.pericope_label: Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners. Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame

schools.summary: Gill names two sources of the deceit warned against, those who deny the doctrine of the resurrection and reason about it, and the libertines who go into the denial and argue from it in favour of their licentious course of life. On the call to awake he represents the Corinthians as inebriated with bad principles and notions, fallen asleep and greatly remiss in the exercise of grace and the discharge of duty, and therefore called on to watch and be sober; and he takes the righteousness named to be the justice of God, which requires the resurrection of the dead so that men may receive the things done in the body, whether good or evil, since it is but just that the bodies Christ purchased with his blood should be raised. Calvin observes that nothing is easier than to glide into profane speculation under the pretext of doubting and inquiring, and that the apostle meets the danger by warning that such conversations have more effect than we might suppose in polluting our minds and corrupting our morals, for which he uses the quotation from Menander. On the exhortation he explains that the original word properly signifies to become sober, a sense it carries in the Greek version of the prophets and elsewhere, so that the sense is to shake off the mental delusion and stupor in which error had involved them and attend with clear faculties to the most important subject.

Barnes marks the change from argument to exhortation and accounts for the danger: there was much that was plausible in the objections to the doctrine, much subtilty and art in the teachers who denied it, and perhaps something in the character of their own minds, accustomed to subtle and abstruse inquiry rather than to an examination of simple facts. He explains the word for communications as properly a being together, companionship and close intercourse. On the call to awake he says the verb denotes rousing from a deep sleep or torpor and is usually applied to those who become sober after drunkenness, and he weighs two senses of the adverb, either rouse to the ways of righteousness and sound doctrine, or rouse as it is right and proper that you should, preferring the second. Ellicott takes the preceding words as sarcasm and then as a description too true of some among them, traces the quotation to a line of Menander modified in one word, renders the exhortation awake to soberness in a righteous manner, and says the whole preceding argument as well as the last words is spoken to their shame, since it was a shame that a fundamental truth of the faith should need vindicating to Christians. Robertson glosses the words for companionship and for morals, notes the iambic line in Menander while allowing it may have been a current proverb, and calls the ignorance spoken of agnosticism, of which some now take pride instead of shame.

Clarke says the maxim resembles many sayings among the Greek poets, that according to the best manuscripts it makes an iambic verse, and that it is generally supposed to have been taken from the lost comedy of Menander called Thais; he sets beside it a rabbinic proverb of two dry logs of wood and one green, where the dry logs burnt up the green, and states the sense plainly, that he who frequents the company of bad or corrupt men will soon be as they are, however sound he may have been in the faith. On the exhortation he insists that the word should be rendered awake fully and thoroughly, as ye ought to do, and not awake to righteousness, and urges them not to trifle with God, their souls and eternity, since life is but a moment. Of the ignorance he says the original is very emphatic, since some have an ignorance of God, a sort of substantial darkness that prevents the light of God from penetrating the soul, which is a worse state than to be simply in the dark. Wesley says the apostle opposes a well-known verse of Menander to the Epicurean saying just quoted, and that discourse contrary to faith, hope or love naturally tends to destroy all holiness; he calls the summons an exclamation full of apostolical majesty, observes that sin supposes drowsiness of soul, and finds nothing more shameful than a sleepy ignorance of God in men who had enjoyed such advantages.

debates: How the adverb attached to the call is to be rendered: Barnes weighs rousing to the ways of righteousness against rousing as it is right that you should and prefers the latter, Clarke insists that it means awake fully and thoroughly and not awake to righteousness at all, Ellicott renders it awake to soberness in a righteous manner, and Wesley keeps the righteousness as flowing from the true knowledge of God

Where the quoted line comes from: Clarke and Ellicott both trace it to the lost comedy of Menander, Ellicott adding that we cannot tell whether the apostle knew the poem itself, while Robertson allows that it may equally have been a current proverb taken from common speech

What state the readers are in: Gill and Calvin picture them as intoxicated and asleep under the influence of error, Ellicott as tainted by the moral atmosphere around them, Barnes as exposed by a turn of mind fonder of abstruse inquiry than of simple facts, and Wesley as boasting knowledge while ignorant of what most concerns them
outliers: Clarke adds a rabbinic proverb of two dry logs and one green, where the dry burnt up the green
Robertson observes that some now take pride in the ignorance of God which the apostle calls a shame
Ellicott takes the shame to cover the whole preceding argument, since a fundamental truth should not have needed vindicating to Christians
Wesley calls the summons an exclamation full of apostolical majesty

35.pericope_label: How are the dead raised up, and with what body do they come? Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened except it die; but God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him

schools.summary: Gill allows that the questioner may be one of the members who denied the resurrection, or a weak believer, one of the babes in Christ who could not digest such strong meat and had doubts without absolutely denying the point, though the manner of the objection and the sharpness of the reply suggest otherwise. He defends the apostle against the law of Christ concerning those who call a brother a fool, since he spoke not in anger nor from a malevolent disposition but out of zeal for truth, to reprove the folly of opposing the veracity and power of God and setting up reason above revelation. On the seed he observes that the sower does not take a stalk in the blade and the ear and full corn and sow that, which is the form in which it rises again; and he insists that it is not the husbandman, nor the sun, nor the rain that gives the grain its verdure and form, its stalk, blade and ear, but God by his own power and sovereign pleasure, who does not create the new form but gives it, and gives it to the selfsame grain. Calvin grants that nothing is more at variance with human reason than this article, since none but God could persuade us that bodies now liable to corruption, after rotting or being consumed by fire or torn by wild beasts, shall be restored entire and in a better condition; and he notes that the apostle, instead of resting on the incomprehensible power of God, shows that the resurrection is so far from being against nature that the course of nature illustrates it daily.

Henry treats the question as a plausible and principal objection against the doctrine and divides it in two. The first part asks how the dead are raised up, that is, by what means, how it can be done, and what power is equal to such an effect; the second asks with what body they come. He observes that the opinion which prevailed among the heathens, and which the Sadducees seem to have shared, made the thing appear impossible in itself, so that the objection is not merely curious but is meant to overthrow the doctrine by showing that no manner of accomplishing it can be conceived. The answer, as Henry follows it, meets the first part by an illustration drawn from what men do every year with their own hands, and the second by showing that the body which rises differs in condition from the body which is sown while remaining the same body.

Barnes says the second part of the chapter opens here, where the objections are met and the manner of the rising is shown, and he treats the rebuke as deserved, since it was foolish to urge as an objection to religion what must equally exist in an undeniable and everyday fact. On the sowing he says one kernel is sown to produce many, and that the body raised will not be the same in the sense that the same particles of matter compose it, but the same in the sense in which the harvest answers to the seed; the form produced is such as God pleases, so that nothing is left to chance. Ellicott renders the rebuke as senseless one and notes that the Greek does not carry the opprobrium of the word forbidden in the Gospel; he counts the three proofs already offered and says the first two are those on which belief must still rest, and is careful to add that the apostle proves nothing here, since analogy can never prove, but only shows how a resurrection is possible and how substantial identity may be preserved under variation of form. Robertson calls the apostle a master at putting the standpoint of the imaginary adversary, observes that we know the how of very few things scientifically, justifies the severity of the rebuke by the objector's self-conceit, and presses the difference between the seed and the plant, since we sow seeds and not bodies and the butterfly comes out of the dying worm.

Clarke thinks the questioner is the false apostle at Corinth, chief in the opposition to the pure doctrine of the Gospel, to whom the letter often refers in this covert way, and finds a peculiar propriety in the rebuke if that man is addressed, since he magnified his own wisdom and set it up against both God and man; he adds that it is folly in anyone to assert the impossibility of a thing merely because he cannot comprehend it. On the growth he marvels at the increase, that out of one bare grain are produced a system of roots, a tall and vigorous stalk with all its appendages of leaves and the full corn in the ear, making several hundred times the quantum originally deposited, and denies that there are any proofs that what some call nature can effect this. Wesley states the objection in the objector's own terms and observes that the apostle answers first by a similitude and afterwards plainly and directly.
