He finds the objection inverted by the answer, since death is so far from hindering life that it necessarily goes before it, and presses the last clause further than the rest, holding that the body given is not only peculiar to that species but proper to that individual, arising out of the substance of that very grain.

Chrysostom attends to the tone of the answer rather than its matter. Gentle and lowly as the apostle is to a great degree everywhere, he here adopts a style rather pungent, and Chrysostom lays this to the impiety of the gainsayers. He is not content with sharpness, however, but employs reasons and examples as well, and by these subdues even the very contentious. Chrysostom also observes how the vehemence of the censure is abated even while it is uttered, so that the reproach does not fall on the whole church but is confined to the objector; and he notes the connection with what had been said above, that since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead, the present question being an objection brought in from the Gentile side rather than from within.

debates: Who the objector is: Clarke identifies him with the false apostle at Corinth and finds the rebuke peculiarly apt on that supposition, Gill allows that he may be a weak believer among the babes in Christ who could not digest strong meat, while Chrysostom takes the objection as one brought in from the Gentile side

What the analogy of the seed accomplishes: Calvin says it shows the resurrection to be not against nature but daily illustrated by it, Barnes that the objection must equally lie against an undeniable everyday fact, Wesley that death is thereby shown to precede life rather than hinder it, while Ellicott cautions that analogy can never prove and only shows the thing possible

In what sense the risen body is the same: Barnes denies that the same particles of matter compose it and keeps only the identity of harvest with seed, Robertson presses the difference between seed and plant, and Wesley holds that the body given is proper to that individual and arises out of the substance of that very grain
outliers: Lightfoot notes that the Talmudists used the same word for fool, and that Rabban Jochanan ben Zakkai so answered the Boethusians, who also denied the resurrection
Robertson remarks that sceptics pose as the intelligentsia, though the pose does not make a man intelligent
Gill defends the apostle against the law of Christ concerning those who call a brother a fool
Clarke denies that what some call nature can account for the increase of a single grain

39.pericope_label: All flesh is not the same flesh; there are celestial bodies and bodies terrestrial; one star differeth from another star in glory

schools.summary: Gill allows what all flesh has in common, that it is flesh as to nature and substance, agrees in its original by generation, is supported by food and is alike frail and mortal, rising out of the grass or maintained by it and withering like it; but he denies that all flesh is of equal worth, value and excellency, since the flesh of men is animated by a rational soul and is set first in the apostle's order. Of the heavenly bodies he notes that the sun is the greater light, the fountain of light, whose glory exceeds that of the other heavenly bodies. Calvin explains the comparison as showing that under the one name of flesh the body of a man and of a beast are both comprehended, the substance being the same while there is a difference of quality, and he draws the general conclusion that whatever diversity we see within any particular kind is a sort of prelude of the resurrection, since God clearly shows thereby that it is no difficult thing with him to renew our bodies by changing their present condition. On the differing glories of the heavenly bodies he warns against a mistake commonly fallen into in the application, for it is supposed that the apostle meant to teach that after the resurrection the saints will have different degrees of honour, whereas that is not what the similitude is brought to prove.

Barnes says these verses are designed to answer the question with what bodies the dead come, and that the argument is drawn from the many kinds of bodies which exist, all of them bodies and yet partaking of different qualities, forms and properties, so that it is not absurd to suppose God may transform the human body and raise it with somewhat different properties in the future world. He sets the two classes before the reader, the splendour of the sun and moon and stars in the heavens and the bodies of men and brutes and insects on the earth, and then marks a further step, since within the heavenly class itself the bodies differ from each other in magnitude, brightness and beauty. Ellicott renders the first clause that there is no flesh the same flesh, allows that all organisms have the same basis and a structural unit runs through all animal life, and argues that the divine prescience which fits each kind to its own surroundings can give another form hereafter suited to new ones; he reports and sets aside the view that the celestial bodies here are those of angels, and states the force of all three analogies, that identity of matter is preserved amid variety of form. Robertson observes that variety exists along with kinship so that even evolution would leave the argument valid, and adds that the telescope has given the illustration of the stars more force.

Clarke insists that though the organization of all animals is in its general principles the same, no two different kinds have flesh of the same flavour, whether the animal be beast, fowl or fish, and that the same holds among vegetables; against those who maintain that fish is not flesh, and so eat it when the flesh of quadrupeds and fowls is forbidden them, he answers that they might as well tell us a lily is not a vegetable. On the celestial and terrestrial bodies he denies that the apostle uses those terms as we do, since we mean by the first the sun, moon, planets and stars and by the second masses of inanimate matter, whereas the apostle speaks of human beings, some clothed with celestial and some with terrestrial bodies; the celestial he takes for such refined bodies as those in which Enoch, Elijah and Christ himself appear in the realms of glory. Of the differing glories he notes the descent from sun to moon, from moon to planets and from planets to stars, and even among the fixed stars a difference of splendour, which may proceed from their different magnitudes or from the comparative nearness of some to our earth, though which cause we cannot tell. Wesley states the argument in brief, that earthy bodies differ from earthy and heavenly from heavenly, so that it is no wonder if heavenly differ from earthy, or the bodies that rise from those that lay in the grave.

debates: What the celestial bodies of the passage are: Clarke denies that the words are used in our sense at all and takes them of human beings clothed with refined bodies like those of Enoch and Elijah, Ellicott reports the view of many that they are the bodies of angels but prefers to read the verse as a general statement, while Barnes and Wesley take them plainly for the sun, moon and stars

What the differing glories of the stars are brought to prove: Barnes takes them as showing difference within one class as well as between classes, Ellicott as showing that God is not confined to a monotonous form, Robertson as an illustration strengthened by the telescope, while Calvin expressly denies the common application that the saints will differ in degrees of honour after the resurrection

How far the variety of flesh carries the argument: Gill grants a common nature while denying equal worth, Calvin holds the substance one and the quality diverse, Ellicott finds a structural unit under all the forms, and Robertson says variety and kinship stand together so that even evolution would leave the reasoning untouched
outliers: Clarke answers those who eat fish while abstaining from flesh that they might as well say a lily is not a vegetable
Ellicott observes that if we had seen flesh in one form only we might have asked with what body it could live in the sea
Robertson says the telescope has added force to the apostle's argument from the stars
Gill calls the sun the greater light and the fountain of light

42.pericope_label: It is sown in corruption, raised in incorruption; sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body: the first Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a quickening spirit

schools.summary: Gill says the risen bodies will be as different from what they now are, though the same in substance, as the stalk in its blade and ear is from the naked grain cast into the earth, or as the flesh of men from that of beasts and fishes and birds, or as celestial bodies from terrestrial. He traces the dishonour of the sown body to its very original, since it is conceived in sin and shapen in iniquity, and when born is in a condition to be loathed, some of its members being less honourable and so uncomely as always to need a covering, and it is subject to blemishes and defects. The natural body he calls an animal one, generated as animals are, supported with food as they are, and dying at last as they do. Calvin says the apostle now explains himself by unfolding the difference between the present condition of the body and that which will follow the resurrection, and he uses that unfolding to settle an earlier question: what connection would the discourse have if the apostle had intended, in the foregoing comparison, to distinguish between different degrees of future glory among the saints? There can therefore be no doubt that he has been following out one subject throughout. Since he could not enumerate the particulars one by one, he sums them all in a single word by calling the present body natural, quoting Scripture for it lest the teaching should seem a new contrivance of his own.

Barnes explains each contrast in turn: the body is sown in the grave, in a form tending to decay and with a kind of ignominy attending it as under the curse of God, and is raised in honour and beauty, the curse removed. The word rendered natural he takes to denote what is endowed with animal life, having breath and vitality, and applicable to any living thing, whether brute or man. Of the quotation he notes that only part of the verse is used and that the words first and Adam are added to designate whom the apostle meant. Ellicott states what the analogies establish, that identity is preserved amid ever-varying form, so that a change in the form or glory of our organism is compatible with the preservation of personal identity; and he finds in them a further point, that of adaptability, since the body a plant has as seed suits the condition of seed and the body it has when grown suits the changed conditions. He also reports the rabbinical reading of the passage from Moses, that God breathed the breath of life into man and yet the man became only a living soul, one in whom the merely human faculties held sway. Robertson calls the four contrasts marvellous, the earthly and the risen differing in duration, value and power, admits that the word natural is inadequate though as good as can be made, warns against filling in details since the risen body is not wholly spirit, and calls Christ the crown of humanity.

Clarke holds that the bodies of the dead, though all immortal, shall possess different degrees of splendour and glory according to the state of holiness in which their respective souls were found, and reports the rabbinic scheme of seven degrees of glory for the righteous. On the contrasts he says the body is stripped of all the glory it had as a machine fearfully and wonderfully made by the hands of God, and is raised glorious because immortal and for ever redeemed from the empire of death, the principles of dissolution having prevailed over it before. The natural body he describes at length as an animal one, with a multiplicity of solids and fluids of different kinds and functions, muscles, fibres, tendons, cartilages, bones, arteries, veins, nerves and blood, requiring continual support from aliment and hence the necessity of labour to provide food. On the last Adam he notes that these forms of expression are common among the Jews, who speak of Adam the first and Adam the last and assert two Adams, the mystical heavenly and the mystical earthly. Wesley calls the word for sowing beautiful, the body being committed as seed to the ground, and dwells on the shock of it, human nature in disgrace, raised clothed with robes of light and endued with vigour and activity such as we cannot now conceive; the risen body needs none of the animal refreshments of food and sleep and air, being endued with qualities of a spiritual nature like the angels of God.

debates: Whether the differing glories of sun and stars foretell degrees of glory among the saints: Clarke takes them so and supports it from the rabbinic scheme of seven degrees, while Calvin denies it flatly, arguing that the discourse would lose its connection and that the apostle has been following out one subject from the beginning

How much the word natural will bear: Barnes takes it of what is endowed with animal life and breath, Clarke expands it into a full anatomy of the present frame, Wesley makes it a body maintained by food and sleep and air like the bodies of brutes, while Robertson warns that the rendering is inadequate and that caution is needed, the risen body not being wholly spirit either

Where the saying about the last Adam is written: Lightfoot admits that only the first clause is expressly in Moses and answers that the second is written throughout the whole sacred book, Barnes notes that the words first and Adam are the apostle's own addition, and Clarke finds the two Adams already spoken of among the Jews
outliers: Ellicott finds in the analogies not only variety of body but adaptability of each body to its own conditions
Robertson locates the weakness of the sown body in the victory of death and its power in this, that death can never conquer the new one
Gill traces the dishonour of the body back to its conception and birth, not only to the grave
Lightfoot notes how much the Jews say of the Spirit of Messiah and of Messiah quickening

46.pericope_label: That was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural: the first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is from heaven

schools.summary: Gill observes that the apostle, having distinguished the natural from the spiritual body and given instances of both in the two principal men, now marks the order of them, and notes that the spiritual body, though the more perfect and excellent, was not the first. Of the first man he says he was formed out of the earth, and that the word used there signifies red earth, citing the observation that the name itself was given for that reason and comparing what has been written of a clay resembling the colour of the body of men. Of the descent he says the bodies of that man's posterity are houses of clay, earthly houses of this tabernacle, which rise out of the earth, are maintained by the things of it and return to it again. The image borne he takes to regard not so much the sinful image of the first man upon the soul, or the depravity of its faculties, as his image of frailty and mortality upon the body, which is subject like his to infirmity and death. Calvin makes the order a necessity, since before we are restored in Christ we derive our origin from Adam and resemble him, and we need not wonder to begin with the lower. He also records that the Manichees perverted the words about the second man being from heaven, using them to prove that Christ brought a body from heaven into the womb of the Virgin, and answers that they mistook what the apostle is speaking of; and on the last clause he reports the hortative reading while judging that it does not suit the argument.

Barnes finds a due order everywhere observed, the decaying and corruptible coming first and the perfect after, the impure succeeded by the pure and the degraded by the glorious, so that there is a tendency towards perfection which God maintains throughout. The first man he calls a mass of animated clay, fitly named dust and partaking of a nature low, mean, mortal and corruptible; the second is called the second man as being the second who sustained a relation to men that would materially affect their conduct and destiny. He applies the likeness both ways, so that all who derive their nature from the first are frail and mortal as he was, while those who are Christ's will have a body like his glorified one. Ellicott adds the ordered sequence to the variety and adaptability already drawn from the analogies, notes that the words the Lord are absent from the best manuscripts and that the preposition means originating from, and prefers the reading let us bear at the close, since it transports the thought to future glory while throwing light on present duty, the resurrection life being begun in us now. Robertson calls the priority of the natural the law of growth, grants that Christ had a human body while placing the contrast between the first man's natural body and the Second Man's risen one, and resists the hortative reading of the last clause as probably a scribal confusion of vowels, since our attaining the resurrection body can hardly depend on our own efforts.

Clarke identifies the natural body with that in which Adam was created and the spiritual with that in which the soul is to be clothed at the resurrection, and says the first man's body was made out of the dust of the ground while the resurrection body will be of a heavenly nature and not subject to decay or death; what is formed of earth must live after an earthly manner and be nourished accordingly. Of the likeness he says that as Adam was, formed from the earth, so are all his descendants, frail, decaying and subject to death, while as is the heavenly state of Adam and of all glorified beings, so shall be the state of all who at the resurrection are found fit for glory; and he notes that his own interpretation proceeds on the ground that what is said here belongs to Adam in his twofold state, of mortality and immortality, of disgrace and honour, of earth and heaven. Wesley explains why the second clause is not phrased to match the first, since though man owes it to the earth that he is earthy, the Lord does not owe his glory to heaven, having himself made the heavens and shown himself to us as Lord by descending from them. He distinguishes the two families by principle rather than descent, the earthy being those who continue without any higher principle and the heavenly those who receive a divine principle from heaven, and takes the image of the heavenly to be holiness and glory.

Chrysostom is chiefly concerned with what kind of difference is being marked here and why. Having said that the natural was first and the spiritual afterward, the apostle states another difference, speaking of the earthy and the heavenly; and Chrysostom distinguishes the two carefully. The first difference was between the present life and that which is to come, but this one is between the state before grace and the state after grace. He also assigns a motive to the way it is stated, namely that the apostle has an eye throughout to the most excellent way of life, and frames the comparison so as to hinder men from such a confidence in the resurrection as would make them neglectful of their practice and of perfection. The doctrine, on this reading, is not allowed to stand apart from the conduct it is meant to support.

debates: What text stands at the close: Ellicott adopts the reading let us bear from the best manuscripts and finds in it a light on present duty, Robertson reports the same manuscripts but resists the reading as probably a scribal confusion of similar vowels, and Calvin records that some have changed the future into a hortative and that some Greek copies read it so, but judges it unsuited to the argument

What the earthy and the heavenly divide: Barnes and Clarke take them of descent, so that all Adam's posterity are frail and all found fit for glory will be like the risen Lord, while Wesley divides by principle, the earthy continuing without a higher principle and the heavenly receiving a divine one

What kind of difference the second contrast marks: Chrysostom distinguishes it from the first, making the earlier one a difference between this life and the next and this one a difference between the state before grace and after it, while Ellicott and Barnes read it simply as the sequence of natural before spiritual
outliers: Calvin records that the Manichees used this verse to argue that Christ brought a body from heaven into the womb of the Virgin
Wesley notes that the phrase is not made symmetrical, since the Lord does not owe his glory to heaven as man owes his earthiness to the earth
Gill cites the derivation of the first man's name from red earth
Chrysostom says the comparison is framed to keep confidence in the resurrection from making men careless of their practice

50.pericope_label: Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God: behold, I shew you a mystery; we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye

schools.summary: Gill introduces the mystery as a secret which could never have been discovered by reason or the light of nature but is of pure revelation, never mentioned by any prophet or apostle but this one, and perhaps learned when he was caught up into the third heaven; he takes the preface as a mark of the apostle's respect for the Corinthians, treating them as his bosom friends. On the last verse he says the apostle returns to what he had asserted about the necessity of an alteration in the qualities of bodies, and insists that it is the selfsame body the saints now have, the apostle seeming to point with his finger to his own. Calvin makes the whole passage explanatory of what had gone before, that we must be renewed in respect of our bodies, since bodies liable to corruption cannot inherit an incorruptible kingdom and there is no admission for us into the kingdom of Christ otherwise than by his renewing us after his own image; but he adds that our flesh will be a participant in the glory. He calls the point a mystery because it had not been so clearly unfolded in any earlier statement of revelation, and says it is so called to make the readers more attentive, since the wicked doctrine had drawn strength from their disputing about it. On the last verse he holds that the passage distinctly proves we shall rise again in that same flesh we now bear, once it has put off corruption and been beautified with incorruption.

Henry treats the verse as confirming what had been said of the change. The apostle here tells them what had been concealed from them or unknown to them until then, that all the saints would not die but all would be changed. Those alive at the Lord's coming will be caught up into the clouds without dying, and yet, as Henry insists from this passage, not without changing from corruption to incorruption: the frame of their living bodies shall be thus altered no less than the frame of those that had been laid in the grave. The comfort of the doctrine, on his reading, lies in this equality of treatment, since the living are not left in their present condition merely because they escape death, but are made fit for the same kingdom by the same divine act.

Barnes takes the affirmation as covering all the dead and all the living, since a material and important change must pass on both before they can be prepared for heaven, and says the third subject of inquiry in the chapter opens here, namely what becomes of those alive when the Lord returns. He explains the words for the suddenness precisely, the first meaning an atom of time, a point which cannot be cut or divided, and the second the least conceivable duration, and he gives the figure of the last verse as putting on or enveloping, as the soul is clothed with a body. Ellicott notes the formula used for statements of profound significance, observes that the answer no longer rests on analogy but comes as a revelation, defines a mystery as what has been concealed until now and is then made manifest, explains the last trumpet as concluding a series already sounding in warning to the nations, and adds that the risen body must be suited not only to the condition of the new life but to its duration. Robertson observes that a change must come, notes that in Christ's own case it was wrought in less than three days, cautions that the apostle claims no complete explanation and does not affirm that any then living would survive, and remarks that the word for an indivisible moment was the scientific term before the day of electrons and protons.

Clarke calls the phrase a Hebrew periphrasis for man in his present state of infirmity and decay, whose nature is not suited to that place, since in his present weak state he could not endure an exceeding great and eternal weight of glory; therefore he must die or be changed, and have a celestial body suited to the celestial state. Of the mystery he says it is a thing they had never known before, and that the Jews had no distinct notions of it: since flesh and blood cannot inherit glory, and not all will be found dead at the day of judgment, all must be changed. On the suddenness he renders the words in an atom, an indivisible point of time, and as soon as a man can wink, and observes that the raising of all the dead from the foundation of the world together with the change of all the living then on earth shall be the work of a single moment, done by the almighty power of God, who calls and it is done. The last verse he sums in a line, that because flesh and blood cannot inherit glory there must be a refinement by death or a change without it. Wesley says the flesh and blood we are now clothed with cannot enter a kingdom wholly spiritual, calls the mystery a truth hitherto unknown and not yet fully known to any of the sons of men, and exclaims at the omnipotence of the change, asking whether the same power cannot now change us into saints in a moment.

Cyril of Jerusalem fastens on the exactness of the language in the last verse and draws the doctrine of identity from it. He marks how very pointedly the apostle says that this corruptible must put on incorruption and this mortal must put on immortality, and infers that the body shall be raised, not remaining weak as it now is, but raised the very same body, which by putting on incorruption shall be fashioned anew. For the manner of it he offers a comparison and then withdraws it as inadequate: as iron blending with fire becomes fire, or rather as the Lord who raises us knows how. The two things he holds together are that this body shall be raised and that it shall not abide such as it now is, so that the change is neither the loss of the body nor the mere continuance of it in its present state.

debates: What the mystery consists in and how far it is explained: Gill and Wesley call it a truth wholly beyond the reach of reason, Clarke that the Jews had no distinct notion of it, Calvin that it had not been clearly unfolded in earlier revelation and is so named to make the readers attentive, while Robertson cautions that the apostle claims no complete explanation and does not say whether any then living would survive to see it

How much of the present body is carried over: Gill says it is the selfsame body the saints now have, Calvin that the passage distinctly proves we shall rise in the same flesh once it has put off corruption, and Cyril of Jerusalem that the very same body is raised yet fashioned anew, as iron blending with fire becomes fire

Whether the living are changed as thoroughly as the dead are raised: Henry insists that those caught up without dying are nonetheless changed from corruption to incorruption, Barnes that the affirmation covers the living and the dead alike, and Clarke that since not all will be found dead at the judgment all must be changed
outliers: Robertson notes that in Christ's own case the body was still in a transition state before the ascension, being handled and eating while passing through closed doors
Robertson observes that the word for an indivisible moment was the scientific term for the atom, before the day of electrons and protons
Ellicott explains the last trumpet as concluding a series that had been sounding at intervals in warning to the nations
Wesley asks whether the power that will change us in a moment cannot now make us saints as quickly

54.pericope_label: Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? The sting of death is sin; but thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Gill notes that the ancient Jews acknowledged that the words of the second quotation belong to the times of the Messiah, and that the Chaldee paraphrase renders them of the Word of God. On the sting he says sin is the cause of death, what gave it rise and being, since death entered the world by sin and is supported in its empire through it; sin gives death its resistless power, which reaches all sorts of persons, young and old, rich and poor, high and low, bond and free, and gives it all its bitterness and misery. The thanksgiving he refers to a victory over sin the sting of death, over the law the strength of sin, and over death and the grave, which will be the ground of the triumphant song at the resurrection as it is the ground of praise now. Calvin says the quotation is not merely an amplification but a confirmation, since what the prophets foretold must be fulfilled, and this prediction will not be fulfilled until our bodies lay aside corruption. He leaves undecided whether the second saying is the apostle's own or another quotation, and states the argument of the following verse as a chain: death has no dart to wound us except sin, since death proceeds from the anger of God and God is angry only with our sins, so that if sin is taken away death can no more harm us. The closing exhortation he thinks has much more force than a simple conclusion would have had, resting as it does on the reward laid up with God.

Henry takes the last verse as the improvement of the whole argument, an exhortation enforced by a motive resulting plainly from it. He counts the charges: that they should be steadfast, firm and fixed in the faith of the gospel which the apostle had preached and they had received, namely that Christ died for our sins and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures; that they should be unmovable, not carried away from that faith by any assault; and that they should always abound in the work of the Lord. The motive he finds in the doctrine just proved, since the labour is not in vain in the Lord, and it is the certainty of the resurrection that makes the exhortation reasonable rather than the exhortation that supports the doctrine.

Barnes says the triumphant exclamation begins the fourth division of the chapter, the practical consequences of the doctrine, and calls it such an exclamation as every man with right feelings will make who contemplates the ravages of death and then the truth that a complete and final triumph has been obtained over it. On the sting he says the apostle personifies death as a living being who makes use of sin as the envenomed instrument with which he inflicts the mortal agony, and that there would be no death without sin; the victory he ascribes wholly to God, who formed the plan, executed it in the gift of his Son, and gives it to us personally when we come to die. Ellicott refers the first saying to the Jewish people originally, notes that in the prophet the terms of the second stand in the other order and that the word rendered hell means the abode of departed spirits rather than the place of torment, which has produced a variety of readings; he pictures death as a monster armed with a sting and observes that the future is so certain that the apostle can speak of it as matter for present thanksgiving. Robertson notes the change of voice in the quotation, that the apostle has substituted death for a word he never uses, that the serpent has lost his poison fangs, and renders the closing imperatives as keep on becoming steadfast and unshaken, adding that the best answer to doubt is work.

Clarke traces the first quotation to the prophet and compares the Hebrew, the Greek version, which reads that death having prevailed has swallowed up, and the later version of Theodotion, which agrees with the apostle's words; the second he traces to another prophet and compares the versions there in the same way. On the sting he says death could not have entered the world if sin had not entered first, and that it was sin which both introduced him and armed him with all his destroying force, while the strength of sin is the law, which forbids all transgression and sentences those who commit it. The thanksgiving he grounds on what the law could not do, since law cannot provide pardon: Christ has died to slay death and risen to bring mankind from under the empire of the grave, and has given us the victory over sin, Satan, death and the grave. The final charge he explains from the derivation of the words, the first coming from a seat, so that they are to confide in this doctrine as confidently as a man sits down on a seat he knows to be solid and safe, and the second meaning that nothing should move them away from this hope. Wesley says death is totally conquered and abolished for ever, distinguishes the two terms of the apostrophe as relating to body and to soul, denies that any can resist the sting by his own strength, and reads the last charge as steadfast in themselves and unmovable by others.

Cyril of Jerusalem answers the apostrophe by describing what happened below. Death, he says, was struck with dismay on beholding a new visitant descend into Hades who was not bound by the chains of that place; and he turns to address its porters, asking why they were scared at the sight of him and what unwonted fear possessed them. His answer is that death fled, and that the flight itself betrayed his cowardice. Over against the flight he sets the welcome: the holy prophets ran to meet the newcomer, and Moses the Lawgiver, and Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, David also and Samuel and Isaiah and John the Baptist. The triumph of the passage, on Cyril's reading, is therefore not a figure of speech but an event with a scene and witnesses, in which the question where is thy sting has already received its answer.

debates: Where the two sayings come from and how they are quoted: Clarke compares the Hebrew, the Greek version and Theodotion for both, Ellicott notes that the second stands in the prophet with its terms reversed and with a word meaning the abode of departed spirits, Robertson observes that the apostle changed the voice of the verb and substituted death for a word he never uses, and Gill reports the Jewish acknowledgement that the passage belongs to the Messiah

How sin and the law give death its power: Gill makes sin the cause of death and the source of its resistless power, Barnes personifies death as wielding sin as an envenomed instrument, Clarke says sin both introduced death and armed him, Ellicott derives the strength of sin from its being a violation of law, and Calvin traces the whole to the anger of God, which is only against our sins

What the closing exhortation rests on: Henry takes it as the improvement of the whole argument enforced by a motive drawn from it, Calvin says it has more force than a simple conclusion and rests on the reward laid up with God, Clarke grounds the steadfastness on the solidity of the doctrine itself, and Robertson turns it practical, that the best answer to doubt is work
